questions.q: Learning is often seen as the contiguous causal effect of ___ on behavior.
questions.explanation: "learning as in contiguous cause causal effect of experience and the behavior" (Lecture 1: Psychology of Learning)

questions.q: In order to say that learning has occurred, a hidden change in behavior must occur.
questions.explanation: Lecture says learning is an "observable change in the behavior", not a hidden change, so False. (Lecture 1: Psychology of Learning)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a mental construct?
questions.explanation: "mental construct ... includes all kinds of the knowledge, information, representation, thoughts, ideas, association"; skeleton is not one. (Lecture 1: Psychology of Learning)

questions.q: Learning changes the ___ structure of the brain through the process of continuous interactions between the learner and the external environment.
questions.explanation: "learning changes the physical structure of the brain" (Lecture 1: Psychology of Learning)

questions.q: ___ shapes the learning process.
questions.explanation: Lecture stresses blending of cognition and emotion ("emotion also plays an important part") in learning; both thoughts and emotions. (Lecture 2: Psychology of Learning (Contd.))

questions.q: Watson's work included the famous Little Albert experiment in which he conditioned a small child to ___ a white rat.
questions.explanation: Little Albert was frightened by a noise paired with a white rat (conditioned fear). (Lecture 2: Psychology of Learning (Contd.))

questions.q: Behaviorism dominated psychology for much of the early ___ century.
questions.explanation: "behaviorism dominated the psychology for much of the early 20th century" (Lecture 2: Psychology of Learning (Contd.))

questions.q: The state of "conscious incompetence" may be valuable ___ of a learning experience.
questions.explanation: "the state of conscious incompetent may be valuable at the start of learning" (Lecture 2: Psychology of Learning (Contd.))

questions.q: Which of the following is not an outcome of effective e-learning?
questions.explanation: Outcomes listed include "more connected knowledge", "wider range of strategies", reflective approach, positive emotions; disconnected knowledge is the opposite. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Instrumental conditioning is an example of ___ learning.
questions.explanation: Instrumental (operant) conditioning, like classical conditioning, is associative learning (lecture 5 covers associative learning).

questions.q: The three major types of learning described by ___ psychology are classical conditioning, operant conditioning and observational learning.
questions.explanation: Behavioural psychology describes classical conditioning, operant conditioning and observational learning. (Lecture 2: Psychology of Learning (Contd.))

questions.q: According to the view of Watson, psychology is ___.
options: about internal mental processes that cannot be measured and observed
questions.explanation: Behaviourists (Watson): "psychology was an experimental science and the internal mental processes ... doesn't have any existence in the scope of psychology". (Lecture 6: Major Theories of Learning)

questions.q: ___ is given by Ivan Pavlov.
questions.explanation: Classical conditioning is Pavlov's (bell-food salivation). (Lecture 6: Major Theories of Learning)

questions.q: The process by which organisms learn to respond to certain stimuli but not to others is known as ___.
questions.explanation: "stimulus discrimination ... process which organism learn to respond to certain stimulus but not others". (Lecture 6: Major Theories of Learning)

questions.q: Higher-order conditioning is intrinsically weaker than its first-order counterpart.
questions.explanation: Lecture 6 covers higher-order conditioning but does not state its strength; standard texts say higher-order conditioning is intrinsically weaker than first-order.

questions.q: ___ is the process of gradually changing the quality of a response.
questions.explanation: "shaping is the process of gradually changing the quality of response" (Lecture 6: Major Theories of Learning)

questions.q: The works of ___ were instrumental in engendering the dramatic shift from behaviorism to cognitive theories.
questions.explanation: Lecture names Tolman, Bruner and German Gestalt psychologists as instrumental in the shift; Tolman and Gestalt are both listed here, so "All of the given". (Lecture 7)

questions.q: ___ intelligence is the ability to perceive the visual-spatial world accurately and involves sensitivity to color, line, shape, form, space, and the potential for recognizing and manipulating the patterns of spaces.
questions.explanation: Gardner's spatial intelligence = perceiving the visual-spatial world accurately (lecture 8 multiple intelligences).

questions.q: Sternberg proposed his theory in 1985 as an alternative to the idea of the ___.
questions.explanation: Sternberg's triarchic theory "is an alternative ... to the general idea of the general intelligence". (Lecture 8)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a kind of product in the structure of intellect model?
questions.explanation: Guilford SOI products: units, classes, relations, systems, transformations, implications; "symbolic" is a content category, not a product.

questions.q: The connections between nerves cells are called ___.
questions.explanation: "connection between the nerve cells ... synapses". (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: In order to create a ___, information must be changed into a usable form, which occurs through a process known as encoding.
questions.explanation: "information must be changed to a usable form which occurs through a process known as encoding" (to create a new memory). (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: Calling back the stored information in response to some cue for use in a process or activity is called ___.
questions.explanation: "the next process is the retrieval, recall or the recollection" (all three names used). (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: For many with ___ deficits, reading facial expressions and knowing how to respond are confusing daily challenges.
questions.explanation: Social cognition is listed as a domain; difficulty reading facial expressions is the standard description of social-cognition deficits. (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: The Information Processing View of Learning assumes that there are limits to how much information can be processed at each stage.
questions.explanation: "there are limits on how much information can be processed at each stage" is listed as an assumption. (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: The Information Processing View of Learning assumes that information process is involved in ___.
questions.explanation: "information processing is also involved in all activities ... problem solving, remembering, thinking ... imagining". (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: The capacity of the sensory register is ___.
questions.explanation: The lecture table says a lot of information can come into the sensory register for 1-3 seconds, but the lecturer also says "limited capacity" in passing.

questions.q: Most children do not begin to engage in the process of rehearsal on their own until about age ___.
questions.explanation: Lecture: "most children actually they do not begin to rehearse on their own" (slide/Woolfolk: until about age 7). (Lecture 12)

questions.q: ___ provides an interface between the sub-systems of working memory and the part of long term memory specialized for episodic memory.
questions.explanation: Episodic buffer integrates sub-systems and links to episodic LTM. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: Memories of specific episodes of one's life refers to ___.
questions.explanation: "autobiographical episodic memory that is about our life events". (Lecture 14)

questions.q: ___ thinking is the ability to create mental representations of objects, places, events, or people in your mind.
questions.explanation: "symbolic thinking is ... when we create a kind of mental representations of the reality of particular events or particular people in mind or objects". (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: We compare new information to our ___ of the person, place, or thing, so we know how to categorize the new information mentally.
questions.explanation: New things are mapped "against the prototype" (Himalayan mountains example). (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: Which of the following is not true?
options: Thinking is a higher mental process
Thinking is fulfilling a need or problem solving
Thinking is only done in verbal symbols
questions.explanation: Thinking also happens in mathematical symbols, gestures, art etc., so "only verbal symbols" is false. (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: Mental images are ___
questions.explanation: Mental images can be in any sensory modality (images, musical tones, etc.); all of the given. (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: ___ organize complex phenomena into simpler, easily understandable, and usable categories and help to solve our problems.
questions.explanation: Concepts "organize the whole learning tasks or the phenomena and make it very simpler". (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: The lowermost level of Bloom's taxonomy is ___
questions.explanation: Revised Bloom: remember is the lowest level. (Lecture 17)

questions.q: The psychomotor domain of the Bloom's taxonomy is concerned with
questions.explanation: Psychomotor domain = physical/skilled behaviour (hierarchy of psychomotor domain). (Lecture 17)

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of meta-cognition skills?
questions.explanation: Examples: "knowing our limits", "self monitoring", modifying, skimming; "ignoring your limits" is not, so only self-monitoring. (Lecture 18)

questions.q: ___ critical thinking skill helps you analyze and process information to come to an unbiased conclusion.
questions.explanation: "open-mindedness ... objectivity without any bias ... unbiased conclusion, unbiased observation". (Lecture 18)

questions.q: The inspiration phase of the creative thinking process refers to the ___ stage.
questions.explanation: "we start preparation, preparation that means that is called the initial inspiration phase". (Lecture 19)

questions.q: Which of the following is true about motivation?
options: It has a willingness to activate but not channel the attitudes of learners
questions.explanation: L21 slide: motivation is a mental (not physical) impulse, an internal process, with 'willingness to activate, mobilize, channel and direct' - so A-C are false.

questions.q: The term "motivation" comes from a ___ word.
questions.explanation: L21: 'motivation has come from the Latin word movere, to move'.

questions.q: It is called extrinsic motivation if causal factor is ___.
questions.explanation: L21: extrinsic when the causal factor lies in the external environment, e.g. reward, social pressure, punishment.

questions.q: ___ motivation is considered to be more crucial for students as it is associated with deep learning, better performance and self-efficacy.
questions.explanation: L21: 'intrinsic motivation is also considered to be more crucial for the students as it is associated with deep learning, better performance and self-efficacy'.

questions.q: ___ proposed that there are three primary drives that drive human behavior.
questions.explanation: L22 slide: 'Hull proposed that there are three primary drives that drive human behavior'.

questions.q: Expectancy Theory of Motivation was developed by ___.
questions.explanation: L22 slide: 'Expectancy Theory of Motivation was developed by Victor H. Vroom in 1964'.

questions.q: An example of ___ is thinking, "If I work hard I can achieve the targets my boss has set for me".
questions.explanation: L22 slide: 'Expectancy is the belief that if we work hard (effort) we will be able to hit the target'.

questions.q: In SMART goals, T stands for ___.
questions.explanation: L23: SMART - '...realistic, time based, it has some stipulated time'.

questions.q: Friendship is a ___ need in Maslow's hierarchy.
questions.explanation: L24: third tier is love/belongingness - 'want to be a member of the group... to care for others and to be cared by others'.

questions.q: ___ theory differentiates between autonomous motivation and controlled motivation.
questions.explanation: L24: 'self determination theory differences between the autonomous motivation and control motivation'.

questions.q: According to Daniel Goleman, ___ handle relationships with others.
questions.explanation: L26 slide: EI encompasses personal competencies 'as well as how we handle relationships with others (Empathy and Social Skills)'.

questions.q: Emotional intelligence can be considered a type of ___ intelligence.
questions.explanation: L26: EI 'is a type of social intelligence'.

questions.q: Noticing a difficult emotion and slowing down or resisting any impulsive action that may follow highlights ___ component of emotional intelligence.
questions.explanation: L27/L28: self-regulation/self-management = keeping disruptive emotions and impulses in check, slowing down before acting.

questions.q: The following are signs of emotional intelligence, except ___.
options: ability to manage emotions in difficult situations
questions.explanation: L27: EI signs include 'being able to move on after making a mistake'; holding onto mistakes is not a sign.

questions.q: Perceiving emotions means ___.
options: Understanding only what somebody is saying to you
Understanding both verbal and nonverbal signals
questions.explanation: L27: perceiving emotions means understanding verbal and nonverbal signals (body language, facial expressions).

questions.q: ___ suggests that 10 distinct components provide the scaffolding of emotionally and socially intelligent behaviors.
questions.explanation: L27: 'Bar-On suggests that the 10 distinct components provide the scaffolding of the emotionally and socially intelligent behavior'.

questions.q: Which of the following is a facilitator of EQ?
questions.explanation: L28 slide: 'Self-actualization, independence, social responsibility, optimism, and happiness... reframed as facilitators of EQ (Bar-On)'.

questions.q: ___ is a strategy for improving one's self-awareness.
questions.explanation: L28 slide 'Strategies for improving one's Self-awareness': '...Pursue one's passions and do what makes one happy... Use positive self-talk... growth mindset'.

questions.q: Having students create autobiographies is an example of creating opportunities for ___.
questions.explanation: Not found in the L26-30 transcripts or sampled slides; writing autobiographies is a reflective 'thinking about one's own thinking/experience' activity, i.e. metacognition; the other options clearly don't fit.

questions.q: Which of the following is not true about management of emotions?
options: It is essentially a private act
It is directly regulated by others
It is influenced by cultural norms
It is influenced by what society defines as appropriate to feel and express
questions.explanation: L29: 'the management of emotion is essentially private act... culture specific... what is appropriate to feel and express... we are not regulated' by others.

questions.q: Simon defined learning as changes in a system that result in ___ over time on tasks similar to those done previously.
questions.explanation: L31 slide: 'Simon defined learning as changes in a system that result in improved performance over time on tasks similar to those done previously'.

questions.q: Robert Gagne defined learning as ___.
options: a change in human disposition or capacity
a change that persists over a period of time
a change not simply ascribable to processes of growth
questions.explanation: L31: Gagne - 'change in human disposition or capacity that persists over a period of time and is not simply ascribable to processes of growth' - all three parts.

questions.q: Psychomotor skills are ___ skills.
questions.explanation: L31: psychomotor objectives are physical/movement skills (reflex, fundamental movement, physical activities, skilled movement).

questions.q: Returning to experience refers to ___.
options: re-examining experience in the light of one's intent and existing knowledge
using helpful feelings and removing obstructive ones
questions.explanation: L31 slide (Dewey): 'Returning to experience - that is to say recalling or detailing salient events'.

questions.q: Which of the following assumptions does not come under the behaviorist orientation to learning?
options: Differences between individuals are important as they will affect learning
Observable behavior rather than internal thought processes are the focus of study.
The principle of contiguity is central
questions.explanation: L31: 'difference between individuals are important... individual differences' is an assumption of the cognitive orientation, not behaviorist.

questions.q: Reinforcement can come through sharing of results rather than a reward.
questions.explanation: L31: 'reinforcement can come through giving information, that is knowledge of the result' rather than simply a reward.

questions.q: ___ has contributed to the humanistic orientations to learning.
questions.explanation: L31: humanistic orientation 'has been propagated by Carl Rogers'.

questions.q: In the process of learning, which of the following is not a component of output?
questions.explanation: L32: outputs of learning = competency development, knowledge, skills, attitudinal change, certification; a training plan is an input.

questions.q: Ambience, space and decorum do not affect learning.
questions.explanation: L32: environmental variables include 'ambience', space, 'decorum', noise, lighting - they do affect learning.

questions.q: Role-playing can motivate ___ type of learners effectively.
questions.explanation: L32: for social/linguistic learners 'the teacher can motivate them by giving them some assignments like role playing, group activities'.

questions.q: The word 'pedagogy' has been derived from the ___ word "pedagogue".
questions.explanation: L36: 'it has come from the Greek word... pedagogue'.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not true about pedagogy?
options: It is a method or way of teaching
It is derived from the Greek word "pedagogue"
It helps a teacher understand how learning should be facilitated.
It harms the quality of teaching and learning.
questions.explanation: L36: pedagogy 'improves the quality of teaching and learning', so 'harms the quality' is not true.

questions.q: Pedagogy can enhance the student-teacher relationship.
questions.explanation: L36/L37: pedagogy builds teacher-student interaction and relationships (modern pedagogy lets teachers guide/coach each student); statement true.

questions.q: ___ learning is based on the model that knowledge can be created within a population where members actively interact by sharing experiences and take on asymmetry roles.
questions.explanation: L36: collaborative learning 'is based on knowledge can be created in the group context by sharing the experiences and by playing different roles that is asymmetric'.

questions.q: The Pedagogical Model provides an overview of the learning cycle and breaks it down into ___ domains or phases of instruction.
questions.explanation: L36: pedagogical model learning cycle has 'five stages' - engage, explore, explain, elaborate, evaluate.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a type of inquiry-based approach?
questions.explanation: Inquiry types (confirmation, structured, guided, open) are not listed in the L36-37 transcripts/slides sampled; 'confrontation' is not an inquiry type while structured, guided and open are.

questions.q: In experiential learning, students are engaged ___.
questions.explanation: L37 slide: 'Students are engaged intellectually, emotionally, socially, soulfully and/or physically'.

questions.q: ___ stage of experiential theory by Kolb focuses on planning.
questions.explanation: L37 slide (Kolb): 'Active Experimentation (planning / trying out what you have learned)'.

questions.q: People with a ___ learning style can often act on "gut feeling" and will rely on others' analysis rather than their own.
questions.explanation: L37: accommodating learners 'rely more on intuition, gut feeling, relying on others'.

questions.q: According to the ___ principle, students learn better from animation and narration than from animation and on-screen text.
questions.explanation: L38: modality principle - 'students learn better from animation and narration than from animation and on-screen text'.

questions.q: E-learning is any form of ___.
questions.explanation: L41: e-learning is 'any form of teaching, training or tutoring' delivered electronically.

questions.q: ___ is a feature of e-learning.
questions.explanation: L41 features include 'user friendliness'; the others are opposites of listed features (accessibility, social justice, open learning).

questions.q: E-learning is a synonym of audio-visual learning, multimedia learning, and distance learning.
questions.explanation: L41 slide: 'It is not a synonym of audio-visual learning, multimedia learning, distance learning as these are just complementary.'

questions.q: Which of the following is not a type of e-learning?
questions.explanation: L41 types: text-driven, interactive, simulation; 'physical' is not a type.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a benefit of e-learning?
options: It can accommodate the need of a housewife
People can revise the learning content as many times as they want
It facilitates in developing and communicating new training policies
questions.explanation: L41 slide benefits: suits 'a working person or housewife or a student', content accessible any number of times, 'facilitates in developing and communicating new training policies' - all benefits.

questions.q: Good learners know ___.
questions.explanation: L42 slide: 'Good learners know not only what and why they are learning' but also how (self-awareness).

questions.q: Learners may multitask when engaging in an online course, which could be resulting in ___.
questions.explanation: L43: continuous multitasking 'makes our attention span very short'.

questions.q: ___ learning is the crucial determinant of successful e-learning.
questions.explanation: L42 slide: 'Active learning is the crucial determinant of successful E-learning'.

questions.q: The brain can process 36,000 visual cues per ___.
questions.explanation: L42 slide: 'The brain can process 36,000 visual cues per hour!'

questions.q: For effective learning, online courses should ___.
questions.explanation: L43: content language should be lucid and 'highlight the important things by using the headings, categories, bullet points'.

questions.q: During Covid-19 the world was busy in preparing 1.5 billion learners for the new normal, i.e., ___ learning.
questions.explanation: L46 slide: 'During Covid-19 the world was busy in preparing 1.5 billion learners for the new normal, i.e., remote learning'.

questions.q: To develop learner readiness for online learning, training sessions on ___ are helpful.
questions.explanation: L46: learners needed training on net etiquette, time management and developing study skills.

questions.q: The typical picture of a teacher being a dispenser of knowledge to the students has been replaced by that of a ___.
questions.explanation: L46 slide: dispenser of knowledge 'replaced by that of a facilitator'.

questions.q: In 2018, Global Education and Skills Forum noted that the 'future' teacher would need the 5 skills to thrive in the 21st century. Which of the following is not one of them?
questions.explanation: Lecture 46 slide: the "future" teacher needs 5 skills to thrive in the 21st century, including strong social skills, data analysis, being a facilitator and an external focus. Strictness is not one of them.

questions.q: Participatory education demands ___ so as to build a needs-based approach to teaching.
questions.explanation: L46 slide: 'Participatory education demands creativity so as to build a needs-based approach to teaching'.

questions.q: Students who consider intelligence as a malleable entity tend to focus on their obstacles instead of goals.
questions.explanation: L46 slide (Principle 1): malleable-intelligence students 'tend to focus on their goals despite obstacles' - the statement reverses this, so False.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a principle to enhance student learning?
options: What students already know affects their learning
Students' cognitive development and learning is limited by the general stages of development.
The acquisition of knowledge and skills in the long term depends largely on practice.
questions.explanation: L46 principle 3: cognitive development 'is not limited by the general stages of development' - option c contradicts it.

questions.q: ___ feedback to students is important for learning.
questions.explanation: L47: 'clear, explanatory and timely feedback' is important.

questions.q: Mastery goals are those that are geared towards the acquisition or improvement of ___.
options: Number of students in a classroom
questions.explanation: L47: 'Mastery goals are those that are geared towards the acquisition or improvement of skills'.

questions.q: The vast majority of formative assessment is ___.
questions.explanation: L49 slide: 'The vast majority of genuine formative assessment is informal, with interactive and timely feedback'.

questions.q: Social cognition has a protracted development through infancy to ___.
questions.explanation: L51 slide: 'Social cognition has a protracted development through infancy to adulthood.'

questions.q: Which of the following abilities comes under social cognition?
questions.explanation: L51 slide: social cognition includes 'face processing and joint attention, and more complex ones, such as theory of mind'.

questions.q: Under social cognition, abilities involved in affective processing are often called ___.
questions.explanation: L51 slide: 'abilities involved in affective ("hot"; e.g., facial expression processing) vs cognitive ("cold")'.

questions.q: Social schemas refer to people's mental representations of social ___.
questions.explanation: L51 slide: 'Social schemas refer to people's mental representations of social patterns and norms.'

questions.q: During the earliest stages of development, children are very ___-centric. They see the world from their own perspective and struggle to think about how other people may view the world.
questions.explanation: L51: young children are 'very much egocentric'.

questions.q: A theory of mind refers to a person's ability to understand and think about the ___ of other people.
questions.explanation: L52: theory of mind = ability to understand and think about the mental state of others.

questions.q: The same social behavior in one cultural setting might have a very different meaning and interpretation if it were to occur or be observed in another culture.
questions.explanation: L52: cultural differences - e.g. smiling has different interpretations in different cultures.

questions.q: Social cognitive theory by Bandura focuses on concepts of ___
questions.explanation: L52: Bandura's theory covers observational learning, modeling and self-efficacy.

questions.q: The central tenet of Bandura's social-cognitive theory is that people seek to develop a sense of ___ over the important events in their lives.
questions.explanation: L52: 'the central tenet of Bandura's theory ... is that people seek to develop a sense of agency'.

questions.q: ___ hypothesis suggests that social processes influence how information is selected, organized, integrated, and retrieved.
questions.explanation: L54: cognitive influence hypothesis - social processes influence how information is selected, organized, integrated and retrieved.

questions.q: Sustainability in economic sustainability is ___
questions.explanation: Corrected after checking the lecture (was: multidimensional). L56 slide (Eggert 2009): sustainability as used in 'economic sustainability' (like environmental and social) 'is a one dimensional concept'; only sustainable development is multidimensional.

questions.q: The term "sustainable development" was first mentioned in a book related to the 1972 UN Stockholm conference on ___.
questions.explanation: L56: 'the term has been mentioned in a book in 1972 ... UN Stockholm conference on human environment'.

questions.q: Environmental sustainability focuses on impacts of processes, products and services on ___.
questions.explanation: L56: natural resources affected - air, water, land, biodiversity, human health, ocean environment.

questions.q: Which of the following does not come under social sustainability?
questions.explanation: L56: social sustainability covers labour practices, human rights, business ethics, workplace health and safety; revenue generation is economic sustainability.

questions.q: SDG ___ focuses on clean water and sanitation.
questions.explanation: L56: 'six is that clean water and sanitation'.

questions.q: SDG 16 focuses on ___
questions.explanation: L56: 'sdg 16 is for peace and justice'.

questions.q: On 20 October 2020, the Higher Education Sustainability Initiative (HESI) raised the flag of higher education as a driver for sustainable development and inclusive societies on the first day of the ___ 2020.
questions.explanation: L57: HESI raised the flag 'on the first day of Global Education Meeting in 2020 on October 20th'.

questions.q: Education is related to all SDGs.
questions.explanation: L57: 'how education plays a vital role in all the 17 goals' - ESD is important for every SDG.

questions.q: Successful implementation of ESD requires a shift in focus from ___.
questions.explanation: Lecture 58 slide: ESD requires a "shift in focus from teaching to learning".

questions.q: ___ competency is the ability to reflect on one's own role in the local community and (global) society.
questions.explanation: L59: 'self-awareness competencies, that is our ability to reflect on our own role in the local community as well as the global society'.
